pages.text: Layer 3 · rule-buyers · the sousveillance stack Who buys the rules of Indian finance? Regulators write the rules; RegTrac watches the writers. SROs borrow them; SROTrac watches the borrowers. This register watches the buyers : the interests that flood consultations, get the meetings, and hire the regulators after retirement. Access and influence are documented through published comments, RTI replies, minutes and appointment orders — not vibes. watching the watchers, room three 6 consultation desks 10 consultations tracked 2 open for comments 21 interests registered 32 documented door moves Comment-transparency scorecard The first test of a captured consultation is whether anyone can see what was said to the rule-writer. Stance per desk, as verified on the regulator's own site. Desk Statute Publishes comments? Documented practice Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 yes Runs a Public Comments section; its discussion papers instruct commenters to submit through the website with stakeholder categories, and comments are published there. source International Financial Services Centres Authority IFSCA Act 2019 unknown Consultation papers listed on ifsca.gov.in. Whether comments received are published is unverified — flagged for checking. source Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India IRDA Act 1999 unknown Consultation papers published on its portal. In June 2026 IRDAI proposed a formal regulation-making framework: minimum 21-day public comment window and a general statement of response to comments published by the date regulations are notified. Until notified, publication of comments is not a settled practice. source Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority PFRDA Act 2013 unknown Consultation papers published on the site (e.g. Sept 2025 valuation-alignment paper via PIB). Whether comments received are published is unverified — flagged for checking. source Reserve Bank of India Reserve Bank of India Act 1934 no No general practice of publishing comments received on discussion papers. Commenters self-publish instead (NASSCOM posted its own submission on the Charges paper; Vidhi posted its 2019 PA/PG submission). Individual comment-archives exist only because commenters chose to publish. RTI is the fallback route. source Securities and Exchange Board of India SEBI Act 1992 yes Posts consultation papers and the comments received on its public-comments portal; a board-approved procedure (18 Dec 2024) formalised pre-legislative consultation for regulation-making. source Why the person paying should care: when comments are secret, you cannot tell whether a rule was rewritten for the industry that asked — or tested against the public that pays. RBI's 2022 Charges-in-Payment-Systems paper drew submissions from every major industry body; none were published, and the commenters had to self-publish. A rule made in a closed room still lands on your bill. pages.title: access.html
pages.text: access & RTI Ask what they won't publish Where a regulator does not publish consultation comments or minutes, the Right to Information Act is the fallback. These are ready-to-file templates and the running log of what this desk has asked and received. File at rtionline.gov.in (₹10; first copy of pages free). Template 1 — comments on a consultation RTI Template — Comments received on a consultation paper To: The Central Public Information Officer, <REGULATOR NAME AND ADDRESS> Subject: Information sought under Section 6(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 Why this template exists: regulators invite "public comments", but several — RBI above all — do not publish what they receive. The consultation record is the raw material of policy capture analysis. Section 2(f) of the RTI Act covers "information held in any material form"; received comments are held information. Precedent: comments on RBI's Discussion Paper on Charges in Payment Systems (2022) were never published; commenters had to self-publish (NASSCOM, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy). I request copies of the following information held by your public authority: 1. Copies of all comments/feedback/responses received on **[PAPER TITLE AND NUMBER, e.g. "Discussion Paper on Charges in Payment Systems dated 17 August 2022"]**, in any format (email, letter, PDF, portal upload), including those received after the stated deadline. 2. A list of all persons/organisations that submitted such comments, with the date of each submission and the mode of submission. 3. If any comments were not considered or were excluded, the reason recorded for each such exclusion. 4. Copies of any "action taken"/response statement, presentation, or internal note summarising the comments received and the changes made to the draft in response. Period to which the information relates: **[DATES, e.g. 17 August 2022 to 31 December 2022]**. If the information is held by another public authority, kindly transfer this application under Section 6(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, and inform me of the transfer. Application fee of Rs 10 is remitted herewith / by IPO no. **[NUMBER]** / online. I am a citizen of India. Name: **[NAME]** Address for correspondence: **[ADDRESS]** Phone/Email: **[CONTACT]** --- **Filing notes** File online at [rtionline.gov.in](https://rtionline.gov.in) against the regulator's public authority (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IBBI and IFSCA are all listed). Expected first response: 30 days. First appeal: Section 19(1) within 30 days of non-response or unsatisfactory response. **Log every filing in `data/rti_log.csv`** — the log is published on the Access page. A disclosure that never reaches the public record serves only the filer. Template 2 — committee minutes RTI Template — Minutes of meetings between the regulator and industry To: The Central Public Information Officer, <REGULATOR NAME AND ADDRESS> Subject: Information sought under Section 6(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 Why this template exists: the strongest documented form of lobbying access is the meeting minute. Committee meeting minutes, visitor records and agenda papers are "information" under Section 2(f). Pair this template with the comments-disclosure template to connect *who was heard* with *what they asked for*. I request copies of the following information held by your public authority: 1. Copies of minutes, agenda papers and attendance records of all meetings of **[COMMITTEE NAME, e.g. "the Advisory Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems" / "the committee constituted to examine [SUBJECT]"]** held between **[START DATE]** and **[END DATE]**. 2. Copies of any notes, submissions or presentations made to the committee by industry associations, member institutions or their representatives. 3. pages.text: methodology About LobbyWatch LobbyWatch is the third layer of India's financial-policy sousveillance stack . Surveillance is watching citizens; sousveillance is citizens watching back. Room one (rule-writers) is watched by RegTrac ; room two (rule-borrowers) by SROTrac ; this register watches room three — the rule-buyers. Ground rules Public data first — statutes, gazettes, published comments, regulator websites, press of record. Every claim sourced per row — with dates. If a figure has no source, it stays out. "As of" stamped everywhere — corrections are visible, never silent. Consumer payoff required — every page answers "why should the person paying care". No insinuation without a paper trail — access and influence are documented through meetings, minutes, comment letters and appointment orders, not vibes. What is in the register today consultation desks scored 6 consultations tracked 10 interests registered 21 documented door moves 32 The roadmap (build order from SOUSVEILLANCE.md) Done — consultation ledger. Cross-regulator ledger with the comments-published fact (this release). Done — interests register. Industry bodies, think tanks, foreign lobbies, consumer side (this release). Done — revolving-door ledger. Sourced post-office appointments (this release). Done — RTI playbook. Ready-to-file templates + filing log (this release). Next — consultation-index scrapers. Automated refresh of RBI/SEBI/IRDAI/PFRDA/IBBI/IFSCA consultation indexes (formats vary wildly). Next — comments corpus. Download published comments at scale; file RTIs for the unpublished ones. Then — the diff engine. Draft clause → final clause → which commenter's language appears in the rule. How the layers join RegTrac ↔ LobbyWatch Appointment authorities (Appointments Committee of the Cabinet; Financial Sector Regulatory Appointments Search Committee) are RegTrac rows. The revolving door lands people from this layer into room one. SROTrac ↔ LobbyWatch SRO members are the same institutions that flood consultation processes. A rule that survives consultation unchanged toward industry comments is a LobbyWatch finding; the membership that wanted it is a SROTrac fact. Data & code Everything is CSV-first in the open repo ( GitHub ); HTML is generated from the CSVs. Data licensed CC BY 4.0 (attribute "LobbyWatch / CashlessConsumer"); code MIT.
